clue.text: Member meets elderly fellow in final showdown

indicators.note: things that meet come together, so the pieces simply join up side by side

blocks.note: an arm is a limb, a member of the body
elderly people are aged
a don is a fellow of a university college

explanation.surface: A club member squares up to an old man in a decisive last confrontation.
explanation.walkthrough: A don is an Oxford or Cambridge college fellow; 'in' just places the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Armageddon is the biblical last battle between good and evil, hence any catastrophic decisive conflict.

clue.text: This might determine how things are done - here or there?

definitions.text: This might determine how things are done - here or there?

blocks.clueFragment: This might determine how things are done
blocks.note: surface reading: some rule or authority deciding procedure
setter's reading: a part of speech that modifies verbs, with two examples of that class

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a question about who sets the rules locally or elsewhere; grammatically, words saying how, where or when an action happens belong to one word class, and 'here' and 'there' are members.
explanation.definitionFit: That part of speech modifies a verb to tell manner, place or time, as here and there do.

clue.text: Making grubby writer's group read aloud

indicators.note: reading aloud means speaking it, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: the writer is the setter, so the setter's group is 'my ring'

explanation.surface: Reading a writers' circle's work out loud makes it dirty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer's group' suggests a creative writing circle, but the writer is the setter speaking of 'my' ring, a ring being a group.
explanation.definitionFit: To mire something is to sink it in mud or bog, so the action dirties and soils it.

clue.text: Conducting supplication bareheaded?

blocks.note: surface reading: making a humble plea or prayer
setter's reading: the beggar's hat is held, not worn, so the head is uncovered

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for begging humbly literally pictures someone holding their hat, so they would be bareheaded.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes humbly asking for money or favours, the old image of removing one's hat to beg.

clue.text: So-called smart creature - it tells the time to kids in the garden!

definitions.text: it tells the time to kids in the garden

indicators.note: so-called means named this way, pointing to what the name sounds like when said

blocks.note: a dandy is a smartly dressed man, and a lion is a creature

explanation.surface: A well-dressed animal that teaches children to tell the time outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: Children blow the fluffy seed head, called a clock, and count the puffs to 'tell the time'.
explanation.definitionFit: The weed's fluffy seed head is called a clock, and children blow on it counting puffs to tell the hour.

clue.text: Handy over, prising out Australia's tail and leading

indicators.note: the tail is the end, so only the final letter is kept
prising out levers one thing out of its place, leaving room for the replacement

blocks.note: something on tap is readily available, to hand
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over
the final letter of the country's name

explanation.surface: A cricket over that dislodges the Australian tail-enders and puts a side ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the tail is the weak lower batting order, so the surface is about bowling Australia out; here the over's O replaces the A in a phrase meaning handy.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on top is to be in the lead, ahead of rivals in a contest.

clue.text: Fervent low wail

blocks.note: first meaning: eager, enthusiastic
second meaning: a mournful lament for the dead, especially in Ireland

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, a passionate quiet moan, but it splits into an adjective and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for eager enthusiasm and a noun for an Irish funeral lament sung over the dead.

clue.text: Sent English Commander-in-Chief to engage immediately

indicators.note: to engage is to take on or hold, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
CIC is the abbreviation for Commander-in-Chief
stat is medical jargon for at once

explanation.surface: An English general was dispatched to join battle without delay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent' reads as a verb of dispatch, but it is the adjective meaning thrilled, as in a performance that 'sent' the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sent is an informal adjective for being transported with delight, carried away with joy.

clue.text: Less than perfect devious sons aren't commonly taken in

definitions.note: a noun phrase used predicatively, as in 'they are no saints'

indicators.note: devious means deviating from the straight path, so the letters wander out of order
taken in means absorbed inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written
ain't is the colloquial form of aren't

explanation.surface: Scheming sons are hardly perfect, and nobody is fooled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonly' marks informal speech, so aren't becomes ain't; it sits inside the rearranged sons.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying people are no saints means they have faults and are far from morally flawless.

clue.text: Terribly ill in quarters, squaddie initially gets drugs

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the first letter is kept
terribly means badly, so the letters are rearranged in bad order

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A very sick soldier in barracks is first given medication.
explanation.walkthrough: A squaddie is British slang for a private soldier; 'quarters' looks like barracks but supplies letters, and 'in' is fodder too.
explanation.definitionFit: Tranquillisers are sedative medicines given to calm anxiety, a class of pharmaceutical drugs.

clue.text: Scorer taken aback by rapid review

indicators.note: to be taken aback is literally to be pushed backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: read right to left across the two words, the letters are inside

explanation.surface: A goalscorer is startled by a quick look back at the match footage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scorer' suggests sport, but here it means someone who writes musical scores; read 'rapid review' backwards and VERDI sits across the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi composed operas, and a composer writes scores, so he is a scorer in the musical sense.

clue.text: Russian plotters essentially bungled - they get exposed

indicators.note: the essence is the core, so only the central letters are kept
a bungled job is botched and messed up, so the letters end up in disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
the two central letters of the eight-letter word

explanation.surface: A Russian conspiracy collapsed, and the conspirators were unmasked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exposed' seems to mean the plotters were found out, but the definition is literal: people who show bare skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturists practise going without clothes, so their bodies are literally exposed to the air and onlookers.

clue.text: Frenchman with brogue's half Welsh

indicators.note: half of a word means keeping only part of its letters, here the closing ones
with means alongside, so one piece is joined to the next

blocks.note: René is a common French first name
the back half of the six-letter word

explanation.surface: A Frenchman whose accent is half Welsh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh' looks like nationality, but as a verb to welsh is to back out of a promise; RENEGUE is a less common spelling of renege.
explanation.definitionFit: To welsh on a deal is to break your word and fail to pay, exactly what reneging means.

clue.text: Language using play on words: "setter's on strike"

indicators.note: placed on means placed after in an across entry, so one piece follows the other

blocks.note: a pun is wordplay
a jab is a quick punch
the setter refers to themself as I; setter's = setter is

explanation.surface: A wordplay-based language, with the crossword compiler going on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On strike' suggests industrial action, but strike is a punch and 'setter's on' puts I after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Punjabi is a major Indo-Aryan tongue spoken in the Punjab region of India and Pakistan.

clue.text: Behind vehicle I caught 11 stripped off for illustrator

indicators.note: stripping off removes outer layers, so the first and last letters go
what comes behind follows on, so the rest is attached after the opening piece

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
taken as written
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the answer to 11 across with its outer letters removed

explanation.surface: Behind a car, I spotted a naked nudist, which suited an illustrator.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 across is NATURISTS; 'stripped off' is apt for nudists and here means their first and last letters are removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A caricaturist draws exaggerated comic portraits, a particular kind of artist producing illustrations.

clue.text: Writes off what's surrounding opening in wood

indicators.note: surrounding means enclosing on all sides, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: in dialect 'as' serves as a relative pronoun meaning what or who
a mortise is a slot cut in timber to take a tenon joint

explanation.surface: A carpenter discards whatever is round a hole in the timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's surrounding' reads as one idea, but 'what' gives AS and ''s' is 'is'; the mortise is a carpentry slot.
explanation.definitionFit: To amortise a debt or asset is to reduce it gradually over time, which is writing off its value in instalments.

clue.text: Expert heading to officer convention

indicators.note: heading means going at the front, so the first piece leads the rest

blocks.note: a pro is a professional, an expert
taken as written
Col is the abbreviation for colonel, an officer

explanation.surface: A specialist is on the way to a meeting of officers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading to' looks like travel, but 'heading' just puts the expert first and 'to' is taken as it stands.
explanation.definitionFit: Protocol is the accepted code of correct behaviour and procedure, a set of established customs.

clue.text: When sailors adopting uniform indicates hostilities

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in as one's own, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: as can mean when, as in 'as he arrived'
old salts are seasoned sailors
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Sailors putting on their uniforms signals that war is coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like naval dress, but it is the radio code word for the letter U.
explanation.definitionFit: Assaults are violent attacks, and hostilities is a word for acts of fighting or warfare.

clue.text: Putin's puppets perhaps, being full of themselves

definitions.text: Putin's puppets perhaps, being full of themselves

blocks.note: surface reading: the Kremlin leader's political stooges
setter's reading: nesting toys from his country, each containing smaller copies of itself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Full of themselves' suggests arrogant politicians, but literally describes the nested wooden figures, each holding a smaller one; 'puppets' becomes playthings from Putin's country.
explanation.definitionFit: Matryoshka nesting toys from Russia are hollow wooden figures that open to reveal smaller ones inside.

clue.text: Show collection of jumbos?

blocks.note: first meaning: to display or flaunt
second meaning: the collective noun for a group of elephants

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumbos' suggests jet aircraft, but here means elephants, Jumbo being a famous elephant's name; the question mark flags the playful collective noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means to display something proudly, and is also the collective term for a group of elephants.

clue.text: Rehearses riddles

blocks.note: first meaning: practises routines repeatedly
second meaning: pierces with many holes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddles' looks like a noun for puzzles, but it is a verb, to riddle something with holes.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are verbs: training through repeated practice, and boring holes into something with a tool.

clue.text: Frightfully posh eat here

indicators.note: frightful means awful and upsetting, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Terribly refined people dine in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a genteel café where very proper folk take tea, and 'Frightfully' is the stock word of an upper-class speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A small café serving cakes and pots of tea is traditionally a genteel, refined place to have a light meal.

clue.text: Old man stifles fire discovered in shopping centre

indicators.note: dis-covered means with its cover taken off, so the outer letters go and the middle stays
to stifle is to smother, wrapping something up so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: Pa is an informal word for father
fire is BLAZE, keeping its inner letters

explanation.surface: A father puts out a fire found in the mall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is father, not an elderly person; 'discovered' means uncovered rather than found.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaza is a public square, and in American usage also a shopping mall or retail complex.

clue.text: Time locks guarding home into which one could disappear?

indicators.note: a guard surrounds what it protects, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
locks are tresses of hair
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Time locks securing a house, a place into which someone might vanish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time locks' looks like a single security device; split it into T and locks of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: To vanish into thin air is the idiom for disappearing without a trace, so the phrase is where one goes.

clue.text: Rogue landscapers stripping borders of plants: their days are numbered!

indicators.note: the borders of something are its edges, so only its outer letters are taken
stripping takes something away, so those letters are removed
a rogue goes astray and misbehaves, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Rogue gardeners rip out the edging plants, and their time is running out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Their days are numbered' looks like a threat to the gardeners, but is a literal description of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Calendars set out each day of the year with a printed number, so their days really do carry numbers.

clue.text: Story going round about parent could be spam?

indicators.note: going round means turning to face the other way, so the letters run backwards
about means around, so one piece is placed round another

blocks.note: a lie is a made-up story
Ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A rumour circulating about a parent might be junk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spam' looks like a dismissive word for the rumour, but it is the example that points to the answer; the question mark flags that.
explanation.definitionFit: Spam is unsolicited junk electronic mail, so an electronic message could be an instance of it.

clue.text: Rich Liberal, leading force, wanting power

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so that letter is missing
what leads goes in front, so the first piece is placed before the next

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal
to force something is to push it
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A wealthy Liberal at the head of a movement who no longer wields any influence.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the P from PUSH and put L in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Lush and rich both describe luxuriant, abundant growth or opulent, luxurious surroundings.

clue.text: Result of getting rash possibly from confounded pests - fleas!

indicators.note: confounded means confused and mixed up, so the letters are muddled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Coming out in spots, perhaps because of wretched fleas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like a skin outbreak from flea bites, but it means reckless.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting recklessly often leads to blunders and mistakes, so missteps are a likely consequence of hasty behaviour.
